question: In the Claude Code 101 course, how is Claude Code accurately defined?
options: An agentic coding tool that understands your codebase, edits files, runs terminal commands, and integrates with your existing developer tools
A C++ language compiler that only runs on Linux operating systems
A utility used solely to autocomplete keywords character by character in a web browser
A cloud storage service that replaces GitHub and GitLab
explanation: According to Lesson 1.1: 'Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that understands your codebase, edits your files, runs commands, and integrates with your existing developer tools to help you get things done faster.'

question: Which environments and platforms is Claude Code currently available on?
options: In the Terminal, Visual Studio Code (VS Code), the Claude Desktop app, on the web, and in JetBrains IDEs
Exclusively in the Windows 95 Command Prompt window
Only inside Adobe Photoshop image editing software
Only on mainframe servers without a graphical user interface
explanation: According to Lesson 1.1: 'It's available in your terminal, Visual Studio Code, the Claude Desktop app, on the web, and in JetBrains IDEs.'

question: What is the key differentiator that separates Claude Code from the traditional chat interface on `Claude.ai`?
options: Claude Code operates as an AI Agent with direct access to your files, terminal, and entire codebase to perform work directly instead of making you copy-paste code back and forth
`Claude.ai` can directly edit files on your hard drive, whereas Claude Code cannot
Claude Code does not use a large language model (LLM) and only uses regular expressions (Regex)
Claude Code only replies in French, while `Claude.ai` replies in English
explanation: Unlike `Claude.ai`, Claude Code has direct access to your filesystem, terminal, and entire codebase — instead of copy-pasting code back and forth, it goes directly into your project and performs the work because it operates as an AI Agent.

question: According to the definition in Lesson 1.1, what is an `AI Agent` and how does it work at its core?
options: Software that can interact with its environment and perform actions to complete a defined goal, working by having a large language model (LLM) operating in a loop in real time
A static script that runs exactly 1 command line and then deletes itself
An Excel spreadsheet containing fixed arithmetic formulas
A hardware protocol used to connect a keyboard to a monitor
explanation: According to Lesson 1.1 ('What is an Agent?'): 'An AI Agent is software that can interact with its environment and perform actions to complete a defined goal. At its core, this works by having a large language model operating in a loop in real time.'

question: Which practical tasks can Claude Code directly perform in your project?
options: Reading and understanding the codebase (explaining features, tracing bugs), editing multiple files across the project (refactoring functions and updating all references), running terminal commands (build, test), and looking up external information
It can only read `.txt` text files and cannot edit source files or run terminal commands
It can only run `git status` and is not allowed to edit more than 1 file
Automatically upgrading physical RAM capacity and replacing the computer's hard drive
explanation: Claude Code can read and understand the entire codebase, make synchronized edits across multiple files (such as when refactoring a function), run terminal commands (build scripts, test suites), and look up necessary documentation.

question: In the `Using Claude Code Effectively` section (Lesson 1.1), what are the 3 core concepts you should always keep in mind when working with Claude Code?
options: 1) The context window (finite working memory), 2) You control its permissions, and 3) It can make mistakes (so stay in the loop)
1) Always load 100% of the hard drive into context, 2) Disable all safety checks, and 3) Never review AI-generated code
1) Only use a single file, 2) Never use the terminal, and 3) Never commit code
1) Always write code in assembly, 2) Always disconnect from the Internet, and 3) Delete files every 5 minutes
explanation: The three core principles for using Claude Code effectively are: (1) The context window (finite working memory), (2) You control its permissions (choosing the appropriate level of oversight), and (3) It can make mistakes (staying in the loop helps catch errors early).

question: Why does the 'agentic' aspect help Claude Code work effectively with a massive codebase despite having a finite Context Window?
options: Because Claude knows how to search strategically to locate the right answers within your codebase without having to load every file in the project into the Context Window at once
Because Claude Code automatically deletes 90% of the source files in your project to fit within the Context Window
Because Claude Code compresses all files into `.jpg` image format before reading them
Because Claude Code only reads the very first file in alphabetical order
explanation: According to Lesson 1.1: 'This is where the "agentic" aspect comes in — Claude finds strategic ways to locate answers within your codebase without loading the entire thing into context.'

question: In Lesson 1.2 (`How Claude Code Works`), what is the standard 4-step sequence of `The Agentic Loop`?
options: 1) You enter a prompt -> 2) Claude gathers context -> 3) Takes action (edits files / runs commands) -> 4) Verifies the results and repeats if needed
1) Automatically delete old code -> 2) Write new code without reading files -> 3) Force push to the main branch -> 4) Close the terminal
1) Compile machine code -> 2) Compress the hard drive -> 3) Send an email -> 4) Restart the operating system
1) Ask for the user's password -> 2) Download the entire Internet -> 3) Delete Git history -> 4) Finish
explanation: The 4 steps of The Agentic Loop in Lesson 1.2 are: (1) You enter a prompt into Claude Code -> (2) Claude gathers the context it needs -> (3) It takes action (editing a file or running a command) -> (4) It verifies the results and determines whether they achieve what your prompt set out to do.

question: While Claude Code is running inside `The Agentic Loop`, how can the user intervene?
options: Throughout the loop, you can add context, interrupt, or steer the model to guide it toward your goal
The user's keyboard is completely locked and they cannot do anything until the computer shuts down
If the user touches the keyboard, the entire project source code will be wiped
The user can only intervene by unplugging the computer's power cord
explanation: According to Lesson 1.2: 'Throughout this loop, you can add context, interrupt, or steer the model to help guide it toward your goal.'

question: According to Lesson 1.2, what automatically happens when your conversation and session data reach the Context Window limit?
options: Claude Code automatically compacts your conversation — determining what it can remove or summarize to bring the Context Window back down to a usable size
Claude Code crashes with a blue screen and deletes the entire project
Claude Code requires you to buy a new computer with a larger monitor
Claude Code automatically posts all of your source code to social media
explanation: According to the 'Context' section (Lesson 1.2): 'Once you reach that limit, Claude Code compacts your conversation — automatically determining what it can remove or summarize to bring the context window back down to a usable size.'

question: Which component is described in Lesson 1.2 as `the backbone of how agents work`, giving Claude Code the ability to actually act on your code instead of just taking text in and returning text out?
options: Tools (such as reading/editing files, web search, running shell commands, etc.)
The Terminal window's fonts
The computer's sound card
The screensaver
explanation: 'Tools are the backbone of how agents work. Most AI assistants simply take text in and return text out. Tools let Claude Code act on your code to get closer to completing a task.'

question: What are the four `Permission Modes` introduced in Lesson 1.2 of the Claude Code 101 course?
options: Manual mode, Auto-accept mode, Plan mode, and Auto mode
Root mode, Guest mode, Incognito mode, and Airplane mode
Read mode, Write mode, Execute mode, and Delete mode
Beginner mode, Intermediate mode, Expert mode, and God mode
explanation: The four standard permission modes in Claude Code 101 are: Manual, Auto-accept, Plan mode, and Auto mode.

question: In `Manual mode`, how does Claude Code handle file editing and shell command execution?
options: Claude always asks for explicit permission from you before editing a file or running a shell command
Claude automatically edits every file and runs every command without ever asking you
Claude is completely unable to read any file in the project
Claude forces you to type all the code by hand while it only grades your work
explanation: According to Lesson 1.2: 'Manual: Claude asks for explicit permission before editing a file or running a shell command.'

question: In `Auto-accept mode`, which actions are automatically approved without asking, and which actions STILL require your approval?
options: File edits and common filesystem commands like `mkdir`, `cp`, and `mv` run without asking; other shell commands still require your approval
All OS deletion commands run automatically, while reading files requires permission
Only `git push --force` is auto-approved, while editing files is completely forbidden
No actions are auto-approved in Auto-accept mode
explanation: According to Lesson 1.2: 'Auto-accept: Files are edited without asking, and common filesystem commands like mkdir, cp, and mv run without asking too. Other commands still require approval.'

question: What is the core characteristic of `Plan mode`?
options: Claude only reads files and runs shell commands to explore WITHOUT editing any of your source files, then compiles a plan of action before starting any work
Claude automatically edits all project files first and writes a summary report afterward
Claude disables all file-reading permissions and only engages in casual chat with the user
Claude automatically commits and pushes code to the main branch every 30 seconds
explanation: According to Lesson 1.2: 'Plan mode: Claude reads files and runs shell commands to explore, without editing your source files, and compiles a plan of action before starting any work.'

question: How does `Auto mode` in Claude Code work to let Claude work smoothly without routine permission prompts while still maintaining safety?
options: Claude works without routine permission prompts while a background classifier checks most actions to block operations that are irreversible, destructive, or aimed outside your environment
It completely disables all security mechanisms and allows any malicious code to execute unchecked
It only allows Claude to run commands starting with the letter A
It forces the computer to disconnect from the keyboard and monitor
explanation: According to Lesson 1.2: 'Auto mode: Claude works without routine permission prompts while a classifier checks most actions in the background, targeted at blocking actions that are irreversible, destructive, or aimed outside your environment.'

question: In `Auto mode`, when the background safety check detects and blocks a risky action, how does Claude usually respond?
options: Claude usually finds another safer approach or stops and asks you for the go-ahead
Claude automatically deletes the entire project directory to free up memory
Claude intentionally bypasses the blocker by shutting down the operating system
Claude permanently locks your Anthropic account
explanation: 'When something is blocked, Claude usually finds another approach or asks you for the go-ahead.'

question: Where can all Permission Modes settings be permanently configured, and what important security advice does the course give about skipping permission prompts?
options: They can be configured in the `settings.json` file, but be cautious when skipping permissions — giving Claude Code free rein to run commands means a mistake could be harder to catch before it happens
They can only be configured in the motherboard BIOS and carry zero risk
They must be configured in the web browser's `index.html` file
They cannot be configured in any file
explanation: According to the end of Lesson 1.2: 'All of this can be configured in your settings file. Be cautious when skipping permissions — giving Claude Code free rein to run commands means a mistake could be harder to catch before it happens.'

question: According to the `Recap` at the end of Lesson 1.2, what 4 agentic concepts combine inside the Terminal to make Claude Code fundamentally different from a regular chat window?
options: 1) An agentic loop, 2) A managed context window, 3) Tools, and 4) Configurable permissions — enabling it to read your codebase, take action, and verify its own work
1) Dark mode, 2) Custom fonts, 3) Emoji picker, and 4) Audio notifications
1) Cloud storage, 2) Email client, 3) Web browser, and 4) Video player
1) SQL database, 2) Compiler, 3) Virtual machine, and 4) VPN client
explanation: 'Claude Code combines several agentic concepts: an agentic loop, a managed context window, tools, and configurable permissions — all inside your terminal. It can read your codebase, take action, and verify its own work. That's what makes it fundamentally different from a chat window.'

question: What types of mistakes can Claude Code — just like any other tool — still make if you do not stay in the loop?
options: It might misunderstand your intent, introduce a bug, or over-engineer a solution
It can never make any mistakes because AI is always 100% right
It can only make Vietnamese spelling mistakes and never programming logic errors
It only damages mouse and keyboard hardware
explanation: According to Lesson 1.1: 'It can make mistakes. Just like any tool, Claude Code isn't perfect. It might misunderstand your intent, introduce a bug, or over-engineer a solution. Staying in the loop helps you catch these early.'

question: To start a Claude Code session in the Terminal for a specific project, which directory should you open and what command should you run?
options: Open the root directory of your project and run `claude`
Open `C:\Windows\System32` and run `start-ai`
Stand in any empty folder on the Desktop and run `npm test`
Open the `.git/objects` directory and run `python`
explanation: According to Chapter 2: 'Open the root directory of your project and run `claude`.' This gives Claude Code the accurate context of your entire project directory tree.

question: Which keyboard shortcut in Claude Code lets you cycle between Permission Modes (`Manual`, `Auto-accept`, `Plan mode`, etc.)?
options: `Shift + Tab`
`Ctrl + Alt + Delete`
`Alt + F4`
`Ctrl + Shift + Esc`
explanation: According to Lesson 2.2 ('Choosing a Permission Mode'): 'Press `Shift + Tab` to cycle between modes.'

question: When you press `Shift + Tab` to enable `Plan Mode`, what indicator in the Terminal UI confirms you are in this mode?
options: The status bar displays `plan mode on` (e.g., `⏸ plan mode on (shift+tab to cycle)`)
All text in the Terminal window disappears completely
The Terminal window automatically minimizes to the Taskbar
The screen flashes red with an alarm sound
explanation: According to Lesson 2.2: 'To enter plan mode, press `Shift + Tab` until the status bar shows `plan mode on`.'

question: When in `Plan Mode`, how does Claude Code process your prompt?
options: It reads files and runs shell commands to analyze the codebase and research the implementation WITHOUT editing source files, while asking clarifying questions to construct a detailed plan
It immediately deletes old files and overwrites new code into the project without asking you anything
It refuses to run any file-reading commands and forces you to paste code into the chat box
It only checks your prompt for spelling errors and then ends the session
explanation: According to Lesson 2.2 ('Plan Mode'): 'Plan mode takes your prompt, then reads files and runs shell commands to analyze your codebase and research your suggested implementation, without editing your source files. It will ask clarifying questions along the way to construct a detailed plan it can execute.'

question: According to Lesson 2.2, what are the two use cases where `Plan Mode` excels the most?
options: 1) Planning complex changes / multi-step feature implementations, and 2) Doing a safe code review
1) Quickly deleting temporary folders, and 2) Renaming a local variable on 1 line of code
1) Automatically deploying the app to Production without oversight, and 2) Formatting the hard drive
1) Playing terminal games, and 2) Downloading music from the Internet
explanation: 'Plan mode is great for planning complex changes or doing a safe code review. Many times you'll be asking Claude to handle multi-step implementations toward a feature, and this is exactly where Plan Mode excels.'

question: In the practical `Example: Add a Dark Mode Toggle` (Lesson 2.2), how is an effective first prompt written?
options: Clearly describing the overall goal (dark mode across the entire app), the specific UI location (a toggle switch in the header to switch between light and dark mode), and design requirements (finding a good color palette that works with existing brand colors)
Typing just 2 abrupt words: `"dark mode"` with no further explanation
Typing binary code `010101` into the terminal window
Asking Claude to delete all existing CSS in the application
explanation: The sample prompt in Lesson 2.2 is very clear and informative: 'My app needs a dark mode implemented across the entire app. Can you create a toggle switch in the header that allows a user to toggle between light mode and dark mode? It needs to find a good color palette that works well with our existing brand colors.'

question: In the `Add a Dark Mode Toggle` example, after Claude has run in Plan Mode and presented the detailed plan on screen, what is your next step?
options: Review the plan; if it looks good, accept it so Claude can start executing the code step by step according to your chosen permission mode
Manually type all the code yourself following that plan, because Claude cannot switch from Plan Mode to writing code
Immediately close the Terminal and delete the project
Copy the plan into Microsoft Word and print it out on paper
explanation: 'Let Claude plan it out. After reviewing the plan, if it looks good, accept it and let Claude work through it — depending on your permission mode, it may check in with you along the way.'

question: Why is it helpful when Claude asks `clarifying questions` during `Plan Mode`?
options: Because it resolves architectural or UX ambiguities upfront, ensuring the plan is built to match your exact intent before any code is modified
Because it helps fill up the Context Window faster
Because Claude wants to test the programmer's English proficiency
Because it is a system error when Claude cannot read the hard drive
explanation: Clarifying questions in Plan Mode help lock in design decisions (such as where to store the theme, which library to use, and how to handle edge cases) before writing a single line of code.

question: When you want to quickly install Claude Code via the native installer on macOS/Linux or Windows PowerShell, or via npm, what are the standard commands?
options: macOS/Linux: `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` • Windows PowerShell: `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` • Or via npm: `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`
It can only be installed by downloading a 50GB `.iso` file and burning it to a DVD
Run `pip install claude-101-gui-only` on Python 2.7
Run `apt-get remove claude` on every operating system
explanation: Anthropic provides both the native installer (`install.sh` for macOS/Linux, `install.ps1` for Windows PowerShell) and the global npm package `@anthropic-ai/claude-code`.

question: In Lesson 2.2, when discussing choosing between `Manual mode`, `Auto-accept mode`, and `Auto mode`, what advice does the course give?
options: There's no right or wrong answer — it's whatever you're comfortable with; you have full control to choose the level of oversight you feel confident with for each task
Every developer in the world is required to only use `Auto mode` and forbidden from using `Manual mode`
You must only use `Manual mode` and never press `Shift + Tab`
Only `Plan mode` allows editing source files
explanation: According to Lesson 2.2: 'There's no right or wrong answer — it's whatever you're comfortable with.' You can flexibly press `Shift + Tab` to switch modes at any time depending on the risk level of the task.

question: Why should you use `Plan Mode` when you want Claude to perform a safe code review?
options: Because `Plan Mode` guarantees 100% that Claude only reads files and runs inspection/analysis commands without ever modifying any of your source files
Because `Plan Mode` automatically deletes all files containing bugs
Because `Plan Mode` prevents Claude from reading any files in the project
Because `Plan Mode` automatically pushes code to Production
explanation: When reviewing code, you want Claude to analyze and point out issues without autonomously overwriting the code under review. Plan Mode locks source-file editing, making it ideal and safe for this purpose.

question: After Claude finishes executing a plan (as at the end of the `Add a Dark Mode Toggle` example), what information does Claude provide to you at the end of the turn?
options: You can see exactly what Claude did and how it reached its conclusions
Claude automatically clears the screen to keep how it edited the code a secret
Claude only prints a random number from 1 to 100
Claude automatically closes the Terminal window immediately
explanation: According to Lesson 2.2: 'At the end, you can see exactly what Claude did and how it reached its conclusions.'

question: According to the `Recap` of Lesson 2.2, what are the two most important habits when writing your first prompt for Claude Code?
options: 1) Be as descriptive as possible with your prompt, and 2) Use `Plan Mode` when you want to stay in the loop on every step before executing any code
1) Write prompts as short and vague as possible, and 2) Always disable Plan Mode
1) Only write prompts in ALL CAPS, and 2) Never specify which UI location to edit
1) Always copy-paste the entire source code into the prompt, and 2) Run commands outside the project directory
explanation: According to the Lesson 2.2 Recap: 'When using Claude Code, try to be as descriptive as possible with your prompt. If you want to stay in the loop on every step, you can use Plan Mode to let Claude dig into the details of what you want to achieve before executing on any code.'

question: In `Auto-accept mode`, if Claude wants to run `mkdir src/theme` to create a new folder and edit `src/theme/index.ts`, will Claude stop to ask you for permission?
options: NO — because in `Auto-accept mode`, both file edits and common filesystem commands like `mkdir`, `cp`, and `mv` are automatically approved!
YES — it will stop and ask permission 5 times for each line of code
It will throw an error because `Auto-accept mode` forbids creating new folders
It will allow `mkdir` but block editing `index.ts`
explanation: `Auto-accept mode` is designed to speed up daily coding by automatically approving file edits and basic filesystem commands (`mkdir`, `cp`, `mv`, etc.).

question: In Lab 02 (`plan_mode_and_first_prompt.py`), when running the `run_plan_mode_dark_mode_example` simulation, what is the value of the `files_modified` attribute?
options: `0` (because during `Plan Mode`, Claude only reads and explores files like `app/layout.tsx` and `components/Header.tsx`, asks clarifying questions, and outputs a plan without modifying any files yet)
`15` (because it automatically edits the entire project right inside Plan Mode)
`-1` (because it deletes 1 file from the project)
`100` (because it automatically installs 100 npm packages)
explanation: In Plan Mode, the number of modified source files is always `0` (`without editing your source files`).

question: According to Lesson 3.1, if you take away only ONE habit from the entire Claude Code 101 course to work effectively every day, what is that 4-step habit?
options: Explore -> Plan -> Code -> Commit
Code -> Push -> Pray -> Rollback
Prompt -> Copy -> Paste -> Delete
Install -> Compile -> Zip -> Upload
explanation: The opening sentence of Lesson 3.1 emphasizes: 'If you take one thing away from this course, let it be this habit: Explore, Plan, Code, and Commit.'

question: What usually happens when you skip the planning step (`Without a plan`) and jump straight into asking Claude to write code immediately?
options: You can easily end up spending hours course-correcting later on
The generated code will always be 100% perfect on the very first try
Claude Code will automatically refuse to run unless you type PLAN in uppercase
The project's compilation time will decrease by 10x
explanation: According to Lesson 3.1: 'Without a plan, you might jump straight to asking Claude to write code — then spend hours course-correcting later on.'

question: In the `Explore -> Plan -> Code -> Commit` workflow, what is the easiest way to handle the first two steps (`Explore and Plan`) in Claude Code?
options: Enter `Plan Mode` (press `Shift + Tab` until the status bar shows `plan mode on`), then describe your idea so Claude can explore the codebase and create a plan
Open every file in the project with Notepad and manually paste all of them into the chat box
Run `/clear` 10 times in a row
Run `git commit --amend` before reading any files
explanation: According to Lesson 3.1 ('Explore and Plan'): 'The easiest way to handle these first two steps is with Plan Mode... To enter plan mode, press Shift + Tab until the status bar shows plan mode on. Then describe your idea.'

question: Why is the stage right after Claude presents its plan in `Plan Mode` called `the best place to course-correct`?
options: Because it's before any code is written — you can easily review the approach, change direction, or request edits to specific parts at the lowest possible cost
Because once code is written, your keyboard is locked and cannot be edited anymore
Because in Plan Mode you consume zero tokens
Because Git does not allow editing files after creating a new file
explanation: According to Lesson 3.1: 'This is the best place to course-correct, because it's before any code is written.' Fixing a line in a plan is many times faster and cheaper than having Claude mistakenly edit 20 files and then untangling them.

question: In the `Code` step (after the plan has been approved), what is the single most important factor for improving the quality of Claude's output before it considers the task finished?
options: Ensuring Claude can verify its own work before considering the task finished
Forbidding Claude from running any tests or checking tools
Setting a time limit forcing Claude to finish writing every feature within 3 seconds
Disabling all compiler error messages
explanation: According to the 'Code' section (Lesson 3.1): 'Claude works best when it can verify its own work before considering the task finished, instead of you having to be the QA. Verification gives Claude a feedback loop — it runs tests or checks, sees the output, which helps inform Claude's next decisions.'

question: What two practical tips does Lesson 3.1 recommend to make Claude's self-verification (`Verification`) during the `Code` phase more effective?
options: 1) Call out existing verification tools in the project (such as test suite commands or build scripts), and 2) Add new ways for Claude to check its work back and forth (such as installing the `Claude in Chrome extension` when building websites so Claude can open a tab and test the UI directly)
1) Delete the entire `tests/` directory of the project, and 2) Uninstall the Chrome browser
1) Always test manually by eye without letting Claude run commands, and 2) Close the Terminal
1) Only use the `echo` command to test, and 2) Never use `CLAUDE.md`
explanation: Lesson 3.1 states 2 clear tips: (1) 'Call out existing verification tools' (telling Claude the existing test/linter commands), and (2) 'Add new ways for Claude to keep iterating and checking its work back and forth. For example, if you're building websites, install the Claude in Chrome extension so Claude Code can open a new browser tab and test the UI directly.'

question: According to the `Quick tip` at the end of the `Code` section (Lesson 3.1), if you find Claude keeps running into the same issue repeatedly (e.g., how to run a tricky command or a project-specific convention), what should you do?
options: Ask Claude to write the solution/rule to its `CLAUDE.md` file so it remembers for all future sessions
Write the solution on a sticky note and stick it to your computer monitor
Delete the project and recreate it from scratch
Switch to a different programming language
explanation: 'Quick tip: If you find Claude keeps running into the same issue, ask it to write the solution to its CLAUDE.md file.'

question: In step 4 (`Commit`) of the `Explore -> Plan -> Code -> Commit` workflow, why should you do a quick check of the modified files (`git status` / `git diff`) before having Claude commit?
options: To make sure the commit is a clean point-in-time step on the codebase — free of leftover experimental code or scratch files that you and Claude might have tried along the way
Because Git requires the user to manually open every file before allowing `git commit`
Because Claude Code cannot run `git commit` or write commit messages
To delete all modified files before creating an empty commit
explanation: According to the 'Commit' section (Lesson 3.1): 'Before you commit, do a quick check of the modified files to make sure the update is a clean point-in-time step on the codebase — it doesn't carry detritus that you and Claude might have tried on the way. Then get Claude to generate a commit message in your style, commit and push.'

question: In the `Recap` of Lesson 3.1, how is the role of each step in the 4-step workflow `Explore, Plan, Code, and Commit` summarized?
options: `Explore` gives Claude relevant context; `Plan` creates a plan of action for you to review and course-correct; `Code` is the back-and-forth execution and verification; `Commit` helps you review and push clean code so you can start your next step cleanly
`Explore` is for deleting code; `Plan` is for pushing to Git; `Code` is for reading docs; `Commit` is for installing libraries
All 4 steps do the exact same thing: running `/clear`
`Explore` and `Plan` are only for beginners, while senior developers only need the `Commit` step
explanation: The Lesson 3.1 Recap summarizes it clearly: Explore gives Claude the relevant context; Plan creates a plan of action that you can review and course-correct; Code is the back-and-forth between you and Claude before settling on the final solution; Commit helps you review and push your code so you can start on your next step cleanly.

question: In Lesson 3.2 (`Context Management`), what is the potential risk of letting the Context Window fill up automatically and relying entirely on Claude Code's `Auto-compaction`?
options: When auto-compacting, Claude has to guess what is important to your task to keep — and it can potentially lose important details
When the Context Window fills up, Claude Code automatically charges 50x more per character
Auto-compaction wipes your `CLAUDE.md` file from your hard drive
Claude Code has no auto-compaction mechanism and will freeze your machine immediately
explanation: According to Lesson 3.2 ('What Happens When Context Fills Up'): 'When you approach the limit, Claude Code automatically compacts your conversation so you can keep working. Most of the time this works fine, but Claude has to guess what's important to your task — and it can potentially lose details.'

question: What does the `/compact` command in Claude Code do?
options: Compacts the conversation up to that point: freeing up Context Window space while KEEPING a summary of what you have already worked on
Wipes 100% of the conversation without keeping any summary
Compresses the entire project source folder into a `.zip` file
Displays the list of currently connected MCP servers
explanation: According to Lesson 3.2 ('Commands'): 'You can trigger compaction yourself with the `/compact` command. This compacts everything up to that point. It's handy when you want to free up context space while keeping a summary of what you've already worked on.'

question: What additional information can you pass along with the `/compact` command (for example: `/compact focus on the authentication API changes and database schema`)?
options: You can pass specific instructions telling Claude exactly what information is important to prioritize keeping in the summary during compaction
You can only pass an integer from 1 to 9
You are not allowed to pass any text after `/compact`, or it will throw a syntax error
You pass your GitHub account password to automatically push code
explanation: Unlike auto-compaction (where Claude has to guess what matters), when you proactively run `/compact <instructions>`, you can tell Claude exactly which focus areas to preserve for the next step!

question: How does the `/clear` command in Claude Code differ from `/compact`?
options: `/clear` wipes 100% of the current conversation context (`clears everything`) to start completely fresh with NO summary of the previous session
`/clear` keeps the entire chat history, whereas `/compact` wipes everything
`/clear` deletes all source code files in the project folder on your hard drive
`/clear` and `/compact` behave 100% identically
explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'If you want to start completely fresh, with no summary of the previous session, use `/clear`. This clears everything.'

question: Which command do you use to check what is currently taking up space inside your Context Window along with a `visual graph`?
options: `/context`
`/compact`
`/clear`
`/init`
explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'To see what's actually in your context, run the `/context` command. You'll get a high-level overview of your context usage, what's taking up the most space, and a visual graph showing the breakdown.'

question: According to the rule of thumb (`When to Use Which`) in Lesson 3.2, when should you use `/compact` and when should you use `/clear`?
options: Use `/compact` when you are STILL working on the same task and running up against the context limit; use `/clear` when you are SWITCHING to something unrelated (`CLAUDE.md` and `git history` are still there to give Claude the basics)
Use `/clear` when you are in the middle of a feature and need to remember the previous step; use `/compact` when switching to a different project
Always run both `/compact` and `/clear` together after every question
Never use `/clear` because it will delete your `CLAUDE.md` file
explanation: According to Lesson 3.2 ('When to Use Which'): Use `/compact` when 'you're working on the same task and running up against the context limit'; use `/clear` when 'you're switching to something unrelated and don't want the previous context to confuse Claude. Your CLAUDE.md file and git history are still there to give Claude the basics.'

question: According to `Tips for Saving Context Space` (Lesson 3.2), why should you keep your `CLAUDE.md` file concise?
options: Because `CLAUDE.md` gets loaded automatically into EVERY session; if it is bloated, it eats into your Context Window working space before you even start
Because Claude Code can only read up to the first 10 lines of `CLAUDE.md`
Because if `CLAUDE.md` is longer than 500 words, Git will refuse to commit
Because the longer `CLAUDE.md` is, the dimmer the text color becomes in the Terminal
explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'Be concise in your CLAUDE.md. That file gets loaded into every session, so if it's bloated, it's eating into your working space before you even start. Move detailed guidance that's only relevant sometimes into a skill or a separate file that you reference as needed.'

question: Why do connected `MCP servers` consume Context Window space even when you do not invoke any of their tools in the conversation?
options: Because by default, every connected MCP server loads its tool definitions and schemas into your Context Window; therefore, you should use `/mcp` to disable servers you do not actively need
Because MCP servers automatically download video ads into the Terminal window
Because MCP servers duplicate your entire chat history every minute
MCP servers do not consume any tokens in the Context Window at all
explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'Manage your MCP servers. By default, connected MCP servers load their tool definitions into your context window, and should only stay enabled when you actually need them. Each server adds context overhead, so if you have servers configured for one project that you don't need in another, disable them with `/mcp`.'

question: What is the 3rd tip for saving Context Window space in Lesson 3.2 when you need Claude to investigate a big question about your codebase without cluttering your main session?
options: Use subagents — tell Claude to delegate the investigation to a subagent so it works in its own context window and returns only a summary to your main thread
Run `/clear` after every single file Claude reads
Open the source files in a web browser and search manually by eye
Delete all `CLAUDE.md` and `.mcp.json` files
explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'Use subagents. If you want to ask a big question about your codebase, but don't want the exploration to clutter up your main session, tell Claude to "use a subagent to investigate..." The subagent does the digging in its own context window and returns just a summary to your main agent, keeping your main context clean.'

question: According to Lesson 3.3 (`Code Review`), what is the first and most natural step to review code when working with Claude Code?
options: Read through the work as it goes — watch the changes and ask questions or steer Claude right away if something looks off
Blindly click Approve on everything and push straight to Production without reading a single line
Wait until customers report a system crash before opening the code to inspect it
Print out the entire source code on paper once a month
explanation: According to Lesson 3.3 ('Read through the work as it goes'): You remain ultimately responsible for what goes into the codebase. Reviewing diffs and asking questions while Claude works helps catch mistakes earliest.

question: Why does Lesson 3.3 advise you NOT to only ask Claude to review code inside the SAME conversation session where it just wrote that code?
options: Because in that same session, Claude still carries all the context and reasoning justifying the decisions it just made (confirmation bias), making it more likely to overlook its own mistakes than a fresh, independent session!
Because Claude Code forbids users from typing the word `review` in a session that already has code
Because reviewing in the same session will automatically delete all newly written files
Because a single conversation session only allows sending at most 2 messages
explanation: According to Lesson 3.3 ('Ask for a second opinion'): When reviewing in the same session where it wrote the code, the model already has the reasoning chain of why it wrote it that way, making it harder to spot blind spots. Using a fresh context yields a much more objective evaluation.

question: How do you `Ask for a second opinion` with a completely fresh, objective context in Claude Code according to Lesson 3.3?
options: Run the built-in `/review` (or `/code-review`) command, or open a new Claude Code tab/session (or use an independent `code-reviewer` subagent) to inspect the changes without being influenced by the prior coding conversation
You must buy a second Anthropic account on a different computer
Run `/compact` and then ask Claude if it likes the code it just wrote
Switch the Terminal theme from dark mode to light mode
explanation: The `/review` command (or opening a new session / invoking a review subagent) starts a clean context focused solely on reading the actual diff and source code, unbiased by the earlier coding discussion and without modifying your files.

question: When a Code Review report returns a list of findings, how should you handle them according to `Decide what to do with each finding` (Lesson 3.3)?
options: Evaluate each item and decide: have Claude fix the genuinely important issues right away; create Issues for out-of-scope items to handle later; and ignore false positives or overly pedantic suggestions
You must have Claude fix 100% of every suggestion regardless of how trivial or inaccurate it is
Delete the entire review report without reading any item
Always refuse to fix any bugs found
explanation: Not every comment from an AI reviewer needs immediate fixing: you decide which items to fix now (bugs, security, edge cases), which to defer to a later PR, and which are false positives you can safely skip.

question: In `Check if parts of the codebase were missed` (Lesson 3.3), what common mistake occurs when making changes in a large project, and what should you ask Claude to prevent it?
options: Changes are applied in one place while other related files (callers, tests, types, docs) are forgotten; proactively ask Claude if any other parts of the codebase are affected by this change and still need updating
Claude automatically translates folder names into Spanish
Git automatically deletes old branches on the remote server
The browser automatically clears its browsing history
explanation: When editing code, it is easy to update the core logic while forgetting to update callers, unit tests, or related documentation. Asking Claude to scan all related parts ensures consistency.

question: According to `Try it out after fixing findings` (Lesson 3.3), why must you re-run tests and verify the application again after having Claude fix issues found during Code Review before committing?
options: Because the new fixes applied during review can themselves accidentally introduce new bugs (regressions); re-running tests and verifying ensures everything actually works smoothly before committing
Because Git does not allow running `git commit` unless Chrome is open
Because every code edit erases the contents of `CLAUDE.md`
Because Claude Code requires running at least 100 terminal commands before exiting
explanation: Any code change — even one meant to fix a bug flagged during code review — carries the risk of introducing regressions. Always re-run tests/builds and verify in practice before committing!

question: When using the `Claude in Chrome extension` together with Claude Code during Web application development (Lesson 3.1), what is the biggest benefit?
options: Claude Code can open a new browser tab, directly test the UI it just wrote, observe the results/console errors, and iterate on fixes until the UI works properly
It is only used to block ads when watching YouTube videos
It makes Chrome use 90% less RAM
It completely replaces the need for Git in the project
explanation: According to Lesson 3.1: '...if you're building websites, install the Claude in Chrome extension so Claude Code can open a new browser tab and test the UI directly.' This creates a closed-loop verification feedback cycle for Frontend UI as well.

question: If you have a very detailed workflow guide (hundreds of lines long) that is ONLY occasionally needed for a specialized task, where does Lesson 3.2 recommend placing it to avoid wasting Context Window space?
options: Move the detailed guidance into a `Skill` (or a separate documentation file referenced only when needed), keeping `CLAUDE.md` concise
Paste all hundreds of lines right at the top of `CLAUDE.md`
Duplicate that content into every source file in the project
Put it inside the name of an MCP Server
explanation: 'Move detailed guidance that's only relevant sometimes into a skill or a separate file that you reference as needed.' This keeps normal sessions from wasting context unnecessarily.

question: Suppose you just finished fixing a bug in the Payment system, committed everything cleanly, and now want to switch to building a completely new feature in the User Profile UI. Which command should you run in Claude Code before starting the new feature?
options: `/clear` (to wipe all context from the old Payment task, preventing it from confusing Claude on the new User Profile task)
`/compact` (to keep all details of the Payment system mixed into the new task)
`/context` (because this command automatically writes the new feature code)
`/mcp` (to delete all Git history)
explanation: When you have committed the old work and are `switching to something unrelated`, `/clear` is the right choice to free up 100% of the Context Window.

question: Suppose you are midway through a 5-stage Authentication system refactoring, you just finished stage 2, and you see the Context Window is 85% full. Which command should you run to continue to stage 3?
options: `/compact` (to free up Context Window space while keeping a summary of what was done in stages 1 and 2)
`/clear` (to wipe all memory of stages 1 and 2)
`exit` and uninstall Claude Code
`git reset --hard` to delete all newly written code
explanation: Because you are still `working on the same task and running up against the context limit`, `/compact` condenses the old context into a concise summary so you can continue smoothly to stage 3.

question: When you run `/context` in Claude Code, what useful information is displayed on screen?
options: An overview of current Context Window usage, a breakdown of what is taking up the most space (System prompt, MCP tools, Memory files, Messages, etc.), and a visual graph of the allocation
A list of Wi-Fi passwords for all nearby networks
A graph of CPU temperature and hard drive spin speed
The entire commit history of every repository on GitHub
explanation: `/context` gives a transparent view of where your working memory (Context Window) is being spent, making it easy to spot if an MCP server or `CLAUDE.md` file is taking up too much space.

question: According to the `Recap` of Lesson 3.3 (`Code Review`), what are the 3 core steps for performing an effective Code Review with Claude's help?
options: 1) Read through the changes yourself and run `/review` (or a new session) for a second opinion in a clean context, 2) Decide which findings are actually worth fixing and check for missed parts, 3) Re-test the application after fixing issues before committing
1) Have Claude self-review in the same coding session, 2) Accept every suggestion without reading, 3) Commit immediately without re-running tests
1) Only check variable names, 2) Delete all unit tests, 3) Push straight to main
1) Run `/clear`, 2) Run `/compact`, 3) Shut down the computer
explanation: The Lesson 3.3 Recap emphasizes: inspect changes + use `/review` in a clean context for a second opinion, triage which findings to fix + check for missed parts, and always re-test after applying review fixes.

question: What role does the `CLAUDE.md` file play in Claude Code, and when is it loaded?
options: It provides persistent memory about your project; Claude Code reads it automatically every time you start a new session and appends its contents to your prompt
It is read only once when you install your operating system and deleted immediately afterward
It stores the project's compiled binary code and is only loaded when you type `/mcp`
It is a log file strictly for human readers; Claude Code completely ignores it
explanation: According to Lesson 4.1 ('The CLAUDE.md File'): 'One of the most useful features in Claude Code is the CLAUDE.md file. It gives Claude Code persistent memory about your project... Claude Code reads it automatically every time you start a session. CLAUDE.md files are appended to your prompt.'

question: If a project does NOT have a `CLAUDE.md` file, what limitation occurs every time you start a new Claude Code session?
options: Claude has to start fresh from scratch every session: re-exploring your codebase, guessing dependencies and existing features, and sometimes making assumptions that make it harder to steer back in the right direction
Claude Code refuses to launch and throws `MissingClaudeMdException`
Claude Code automatically deletes all files in the project directory
You will not be able to use the `Shift + Tab` shortcut
explanation: According to Lesson 4.1 ('The Problem It Solves'): 'When you open Claude Code without a CLAUDE.md file, it starts fresh every time. It has to re-explore your codebase, figure out what dependencies are needed, and understand what features are already implemented. Sometimes it makes assumptions, which makes it harder to steer back in the right direction.'

question: In the typical example in Lesson 4.1 (`An Example`), what 3 main groups of information does a clean, effective `CLAUDE.md` file usually include?
options: 1) `# Project` (brief tech stack overview: Next.js, Tailwind, Drizzle ORM, etc.), 2) `# Commands` (dev server, test, and lint commands), and 3) `# Code Style` (coding conventions and directory structure)
1) The full source code of every file in the project, 2) Chat history from the past 6 months, and 3) Database passwords
1) Biographies of all company employees, 2) Annual financial reports, and 3) Holiday schedules
1) HTML source of the Google homepage, 2) Base64-encoded company logo image, and 3) A list of 10,000 English vocabulary words
explanation: The standard example in Lesson 4.1 divides `CLAUDE.md` into 3 concise, practical sections: `# Project` (tech stack), `# Commands` (`npm run dev`, `npm test`, `npm run lint`), and `# Code Style` (TypeScript strict mode, named exports, API route locations).

question: According to `CLAUDE.md is for Teams` (Lesson 4.1), what is the difference between `Project-level CLAUDE.md` and `User-level CLAUDE.md`?
options: `Project-level CLAUDE.md` lives at the project root and is committed to Git to share with the whole team; `User-level CLAUDE.md` lives in your personal config directory (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) and applies across all your own projects
`Project-level CLAUDE.md` only works on Windows, while `User-level CLAUDE.md` only works on macOS
You are only allowed to use one of the two files; the system never combines both
`User-level CLAUDE.md` must be pushed to the company's public GitHub repository
explanation: The system supports a hierarchy of memory files: Project-level `CLAUDE.md` at the project root to share team-wide standards via version control; User-level `CLAUDE.md` in your personal config folder to store personal preferences across all your projects.

question: According to `Tips` in Lesson 4.1, if you find yourself repeatedly correcting Claude on the same thing (e.g., always reminding it to use Server Actions instead of API routes), what is the fastest way to save that rule to memory?
options: Tell Claude directly in the chat: explicitly ask it to update your `CLAUDE.md` so it remembers the rule next time
Close Claude Code, uninstall it, and reinstall it from scratch
Run `/clear` 5 times in a row
Switch the permission mode to `Plan Mode`
explanation: According to Lesson 4.1 ('Tips - Save corrections to memory'): 'If you find yourself correcting Claude repeatedly — like telling it to always use server actions instead of API routes — explicitly ask Claude to update your CLAUDE.md so it remembers next time.'

question: How can you reference an existing documentation file in your project (such as `README.md` or `docs/api.md`) from inside `CLAUDE.md` so Claude knows to read it when needed?
options: Use the `@` symbol followed by the file path (for example: `Please read if you need more info: @README.md`)
Use the HTML tag `<iframe src="README.md"></iframe>`
Use the keyword `IMPORT_BINARY(README.md)`
You cannot reference other files from inside `CLAUDE.md`
explanation: According to Lesson 4.1 ('Tips - Reference project docs'): 'If you have documentation in your project that you want Claude to reference, use the `@` symbol with the file path: `Please read if you need more info: @README.md`.'

question: Why does Lesson 4.1 recommend `Start without one` (starting a project without creating `CLAUDE.md` from minute one, and running `/init` later)?
options: So you can observe where you constantly have to course-correct the model in practice, keeping `CLAUDE.md` compact and focused only on necessary information; when ready, run `/init` to have Claude generate one for you
Because `/init` only works after a project has at least 1,000 Git commits
Because if you create `CLAUDE.md` at the start, Claude Code cannot read source files
Because `CLAUDE.md` automatically expires after 24 hours
explanation: According to Lesson 4.1: 'Start without one. We recommend starting a project without a CLAUDE.md file so you can see where you constantly have to course-correct the model. This keeps your CLAUDE.md compact and focused on only the necessary information. When you're ready, run `/init` to have Claude generate one for you.'

question: In Lesson 4.2 (`Subagents`), if you create or add a new Subagent configuration file to `.claude/agents/` while a Claude Code session is already open, what must you do for Claude Code to load that new Subagent?
options: Restart Claude Code to load the new subagent, or create it via `/agents` directly inside the session
Reinstall the entire operating system
Delete the `CLAUDE.md` file for the Subagent to work
Change the file extension from `.md` to `.json`
explanation: According to Lesson 4.2: If a subagent file is created externally while your session is already open, restart Claude Code so it scans and loads the new subagent into the list.

question: According to `Further Customization` in Lesson 4.2 (`Subagents`), when you preload Skills into a Subagent by adding the `skills` key to its YAML frontmatter, how does this loading mechanism differ from how Skills work in the main conversation?
options: Unlike in the main conversation (where only `name` + `description` are loaded upfront and the full skill is loaded on demand), skills listed in a Subagent's `skills` key have their ENTIRE content loaded into the Subagent's Context Window immediately
In a Subagent, only the Skill's name is loaded while the body of the Skill is completely stripped
Skills declared in a Subagent are automatically disabled and cannot be used
There is no difference between the two mechanisms
explanation: This is a notable detail in Lesson 4.2 ('Further Customization'): 'Preload skills into subagents by adding the `skills` key and listing skills by name. Note that unlike skills in your main conversation, the entire skill is loaded into context here.'

question: Besides preloading Skills (`skills` key), what other advanced Subagent customization feature mentioned in `Further Customization` (Lesson 4.2) helps a Subagent work more effectively when used repeatedly on the same project?
options: `Persistent memory` — lets your subagent retain memory across different conversations
`Auto-overclocking` — lets the subagent overclock GPU speed
`Global broadcasting` — lets the subagent send messages to every computer on the LAN
`Infinite recursion` — lets the subagent call itself infinitely
explanation: According to Lesson 4.2: 'Persistent memory lets your subagent retain memory across conversations. This is great if you're using it consistently on the same projects.'

question: In Lesson 4.3 (`Skills`), what is the core difference between placing instructions in `CLAUDE.md` versus placing them in a `Skill` (`.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`)?
options: `CLAUDE.md` is always loaded in full into EVERY session (for always-needed info), whereas `Skills` only load `name` and `description` initially and load the full `SKILL.md` content on-demand when a task matches or when you type `/skill-name`
`Skills` are always loaded 100% into every session, whereas `CLAUDE.md` is only loaded when you run `/claude-md`
`CLAUDE.md` can only be written in English, whereas `Skills` can only be written in Python
`Skills` cannot be shared via Git; only `CLAUDE.md` can be shared via Git
explanation: `CLAUDE.md` consumes context in every session because it is always loaded automatically. By contrast, `Skills` use Progressive Disclosure: normally they cost only a few dozen tokens for `name` + `description`, and only load the full detailed instructions into context when the relevant task arises!

question: How do you trigger a Skill in Claude Code?
options: Either let Claude automatically invoke it when your request matches the Skill's `description`, or manually type `/<skill-name>` (slash command) directly in the chat
Open `SKILL.md` and copy-paste its entire contents into the chat on every turn
Restart your computer every time you want to use a Skill
It can only be triggered by editing `.mcp.json`
explanation: Skills support both automatic invocation via semantic matching against the `description` field and automatic registration as a `/<skill-name>` slash command that you can invoke manually at any time.

question: If you create a Skill (e.g., a `release-notes` workflow or a sensitive script) and ONLY want it to run when you manually type `/<skill-name>` — preventing Claude from invoking it automatically — which setting should you add to the YAML frontmatter of `SKILL.md`?
options: `disable-model-invocation: true`
`auto-run: never`
`manual-mode-only: yes`
`block-claude: 100`
explanation: Setting `disable-model-invocation: true` in the YAML frontmatter of `SKILL.md` prevents Claude from autonomously invoking that skill, ensuring it only runs when the user explicitly calls `/<skill-name>`.

question: According to Lesson 4.4 (`MCP`), what problem does the `Model Context Protocol (MCP)` solve for Claude Code?
options: It is an open standard that lets Claude Code connect to external tools and data sources outside your codebase (such as project trackers like Linear or Jira, web browsers, or up-to-date documentation repositories like Context7)
It is a file compression algorithm that shrinks hard drive usage by 10x
It is a color theme engine for changing VS Code's background
It is a compiler that translates Python code into Java
explanation: According to Lesson 4.4: 'Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets Claude Code connect to external tools and data sources... A lot of your context lives outside your codebase — in databases, productivity apps, or public repositories. MCP bridges that gap.'

question: In Lesson 4.4, what two real-world examples are given to illustrate what you can do when connecting an MCP Server to Claude Code?
options: 1) Connecting a `Linear MCP server` to ask what issues are assigned to you, and 2) Connecting a `Context7` MCP server to provide up-to-date library documentation to Claude Code
1) Connecting a 3D printer to print computer cases, and 2) Connecting a microwave to heat food
1) Connecting Spotify music software, and 2) Connecting a chess game
1) Replacing the TypeScript compiler, and 2) Eliminating the need for `CLAUDE.md`
explanation: Lesson 4.4 explicitly cites these 2 examples: 'For example, if your team uses Linear for project management, you can add a Linear MCP server to bring in the details of what's assigned to you. If you need up-to-date documentation for a specific coding task, an MCP server like Context7 can provide that to Claude Code.'

question: Which CLI command do you use to add a new MCP Server to Claude Code, and what are the two server connection types introduced in Lesson 4.4?
options: Use `claude mcp add`, with 2 server types: 1) `HTTP servers` (for remote services connected over the network), and 2) `Stdio servers` (for local processes running directly on your machine)
Use `npm install mcp`, with 2 server types: `FTP servers` and `Bluetooth servers`
Use `git add mcp`, with 2 server types: `SQL servers` and `HTML servers`
Use `/init mcp`, which only supports the `UDP` protocol
explanation: According to 'Adding an MCP Server' (Lesson 4.4): 'You can add MCP servers with the `claude mcp add` command. There are two types: HTTP servers are for remote services (hosted by the service provider and connect over the network); Stdio servers are for local processes that run on your machine.'

question: Inside a Claude Code session, which command do you run to see which MCP servers are connected, check for connection errors, and disable servers you do not need?
options: `/mcp`
`/hooks`
`/agents`
`/compact`
explanation: According to Lesson 4.4: 'You can manage your servers with `/mcp` inside a Claude Code session to see what's connected, check errors, and disable servers you don't need.'

question: According to `Scoping Servers` (Lesson 4.4), what are the 3 levels at which MCP servers in Claude Code can be scoped?
options: 1) `Local` (only enabled in the current project, just for you), 2) `User` (available across all your projects), and 3) `Project` (uses a `.mcp.json` file checked into Git so everyone on the team shares the same servers)
1) `Frontend`, 2) `Backend`, and 3) `Database`
1) `Development`, 2) `Staging`, and 3) `Production`
1) `Read-only`, 2) `Auto-accept`, and 3) `Plan`
explanation: According to 'Scoping Servers' (Lesson 4.4): (1) Local — only enabled in the current project, just for you; (2) User — available across all your projects; (3) Project — uses a `.mcp.json` file that you check into version control so everyone on the team gets the same servers.

question: When you configure an MCP server at the `Project` scope to share with all team members via Git, which file stores that MCP server configuration?
options: `.mcp.json`
`CLAUDE.md`
`package-lock.json`
`.gitignore`
explanation: According to Lesson 4.4: 'Project — uses a `.mcp.json` file that you check into version control so everyone on the team gets the same servers.'

question: According to `Context Costs` (Lesson 4.4), why is having too many MCP servers connected simultaneously detrimental to your Context Window?
options: Because MCP servers always load all of their `tool names and schemas` into your Context Window even when you are not actively using them in that session
Because each MCP server automatically deletes 1,000 lines of code in your project
Because MCP servers force Claude Code to disable Auto-compaction
Because MCP servers corrupt the formatting of `CLAUDE.md`
explanation: According to Lesson 4.4 ('Context Costs'): 'MCP servers add their tool names and schemas into your context window, even when you're not actively using them. Each connected server takes up space, so run `/mcp` to see what's connected and disable anything you're not actively using.'

question: According to Lesson 4.5 (`Hooks`), what is `The big difference` between `Hooks` and everything else covered in Claude Code 101 (`CLAUDE.md`, `Skills`, `Subagents`, `MCP`)?
options: Hooks are DETERMINISTIC — they always run 100% of the time without exception, turning your rules into absolute guarantees rather than mere suggestions to the AI model!
Hooks only run when the AI model feels like it, whereas `CLAUDE.md` is 100% deterministic
Hooks are the only feature used to chat with the user by voice
Hooks only work on the Web interface and not in the Terminal
explanation: The opening of Lesson 4.5 states: 'Hooks let you run commands at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle. The big difference between hooks and everything else covered in this course is that hooks are deterministic — they always run.'

question: Why should you use a `Hook` to run a code formatter (like `Prettier` or `gofmt`) after every file edit instead of just writing `'Run Prettier after every file edit'` in `CLAUDE.md`?
options: Because when written in `CLAUDE.md`, Claude will follow it most of the time but sometimes it won't; whereas a Hook guarantees Prettier executes 100% of the time with no exceptions!
Because `CLAUDE.md` does not allow mentioning the tool name `Prettier`
Because running Prettier via a Hook does not require Node.js to be installed on the machine
Because a Hook runs slower than `CLAUDE.md` but looks prettier
explanation: According to Lesson 4.5 ('Why Use Hooks'): 'You can tell Claude in your CLAUDE.md to run Prettier after every file edit. Most of the time it will. But sometimes it won't. A hook makes it happen every single time, no exceptions... Hooks turn your team's conventions into guarantees, not suggestions.'

question: Where are Hooks in Claude Code configured, and what are the 5 common `lifecycle events` listed in Lesson 4.5?
options: Configured in `settings.json` (such as `.claude/settings.json`), with the 5 common events being: `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, and `Notification`
Configured in `.mcp.json`, with the 5 events being: `OnClick`, `OnHover`, `OnScroll`, `OnLoad`, and `OnResize`
Configured in `CLAUDE.md`, with the 5 events being: `GitInit`, `GitAdd`, `GitCommit`, `GitPush`, and `GitPull`
Configured in `package.json`, with the 5 events being: `Start`, `Pause`, `Resume`, `Kill`, and `Restart`
explanation: According to 'How They Work' (Lesson 4.5): Hooks are configured in `settings.json` with common events including: `PreToolUse` (before a tool call), `PostToolUse` (after a tool finishes), `UserPromptSubmit` (when the user submits a prompt), `Stop` (when Claude finishes responding), and `Notification` (when Claude sends a notification).

question: Inside a Claude Code session, which command can you run to open a read-only list to verify whether your configured Hooks are showing up properly?
options: `/hooks`
`/mcp`
`/context`
`/review`
explanation: According to Lesson 4.5: Running `/hooks` inside Claude Code opens a read-only list of your configured hooks, so you can check that new ones show up.

question: To set up the most common Hook — auto-formatting code right after every time Claude edits or creates a file — which event should you choose and what should the `matcher` field be set to?
options: Choose the `PostToolUse` event with a `matcher` of `"Edit|Write"`
Choose the `PreToolUse` event with a `matcher` of `"Read|Grep"`
Choose the `UserPromptSubmit` event with a `matcher` of `"Bash"`
Choose the `Notification` event with no `matcher`
explanation: According to Lesson 4.5: 'The most common hook is auto-formatting after edits. Set a `PostToolUse` hook with a matcher of `"Edit|Write"` so it fires after Claude uses the Edit or Write tool. The command checks the file extension and runs the appropriate formatter.'

question: When a Hook attached to the `PreToolUse` event is triggered, how does it receive information about the `tool name` and `input` arguments Claude is about to call?
options: The Hook receives the tool name and input as JSON on standard input `stdin`
The Hook must read from a screenshot image file on the hard drive

question: In a `PreToolUse` Hook, if your validation script wants to BLOCK Claude's tool call and send the rejection reason back to Claude so it can adjust, what `Exit code` must your script return and where must it print the message?
options: Return `Exit code 2` and write the blocking reason to standard error `stderr` (which gets fed back to Claude as feedback so it knows why it was blocked and can adjust)
Return `Exit code 0` and print nothing
Return `Exit code 1` and write the message into `README.md`
Return `Exit code 404` and power off the computer
explanation:
This is a critical concept in Lesson 4.5 ('Blocking with PreToolUse'):
- `Exit code 0` — proceed normally.
- `Exit code 2` — block the action. The stderr message gets fed back to Claude as feedback so it knows why it was blocked and can adjust.
- `Any other exit code` — a non-blocking error that gets shown to you but doesn't stop anything.

question: What happens if a `PreToolUse` Hook returns `Exit code 1` (or any exit code other than `0` and `2`)?

It deletes the project's `settings.json` file
It automatically switches Claude Code into `Plan Mode`
explanation: According to Lesson 4.5: Only `Exit code 2` actually blocks a tool call. Any exit code other than `0` and `2` (such as `Exit code 1`) is simply 'a non-blocking error that gets shown to you but doesn't stop anything'.
